episode.throughLine: In dated correspondence, a composer asks for more time with an opera text; permission coexists with later unfinished work and doubt. A short source-led account, not a therapy or cure narrative.

contentProfile.contentNote: Creative incapacity and distress, without diagnosis, medical advice, treatment instructions, or a miraculous cure. Source-led correspondence vignette; Russian transcriptions read directly, not collated against manuscripts or the printed edition. New stage proposal matches the actual June 1900–November 1901 boundary and ages 27–28. Same-day letters remain separate documents; their precise order and continuous concurrence are not established. Replaces the earlier 1897-premiere/therapy matching premise. Draft with no recorded review.

facts.statement: Born April1,1873, he was27 in June1900 and28 later in1901.

sourceRefs.locator: Biographical Note, birth entry; ages calculated against dated letters.

facts.statement: On June14/27,1900, he wrote that he had arrived on the11th, now knew his room and had obtained paper and ink amid household disorder and heat; his room was shut.
That same day he answered a letter from Modest Tchaikovsky that had been forwarded from Crimea to Italy and received that day.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening paragraph before 'Since I visited you in Klin'.

facts.statement: He wrote that in two years he had composed only one song, apparently lost the ability to compose, and was intent on regaining it.

sourceRefs.locator: First paragraph, from 'С тех пор' to paragraph end.

facts.statement: He wanted to try writing Francesca again that summer and asked the librettist to defer an answer to another prospective composer until September; if nothing resulted again he would give up the subject.
If delay was impossible, he offered to return the libretto immediately, unwilling to risk leaving its author without a composer again.
In a subsequent letter he thanked Morozov for encouraging advice but still regretted the journey and found noise around his separate room; he planned to stay and work regularly.
By July5/18 he had received permission to keep the libretto for the time being; he wrote thanks and repeated his promise to answer in September.
On18February1901 Old Style he corrected a report that his concerto was complete; he withdrew from a scheduled concert because it would not be ready.
In April1901 he sent two concerto movements to Goldenweiser for review, while doubting the first movement would be finished by Saturday.
In October1901 he played through the first movement and agreed with Morozov's structural criticism; he reported despair five days before a performance.
Rachmaninoff was a composer and pianist whose works include the Second Piano Concerto.

sourceRefs.locator: Collection Summary and Biographical Note, circa1900 entry.

arc.canonicalText: At twenty-seven, he wrote to a friend from the house where he was staying. He had obtained paper and ink amid cleaning, moving things, dust and heat. His room was shut.
arc.sourceNote: Source-led correspondence vignette. Letter157 itself supplies the place, writing materials and shut room. No invented locking action, pose or same-day concurrence with letter158.

arc.canonicalText: In a separate letter that day, he described how little music he had written. Over two years, he said, he had composed only one song. It seemed to him that his ability to compose had gone. He wanted it back.
arc.sourceNote: Separate dated letter158, not a single sitting fused with letter157. 'It seemed' preserves по-видимому: his self-assessment, not a clinical conclusion.

arc.canonicalText: He asked the writer of an opera text to let him keep it longer. He hoped to try again that summer. If he failed, he promised to give up the subject later that year. If waiting was impossible, he offered to send the text back immediately. The writer could refuse.
arc.sourceNote: Conditional request in letter158, paragraphs2–3. No quote, promise of completion or first successful composing session. Opera text and concerto remain different works.

arc.canonicalText: A later letter to his friend still described trouble in the lodging. Noise sometimes surrounded his separate room. The friend's advice had encouraged him, and he wrote with thanks. He intended to remain and work regularly. He still regretted the trip.
arc.sourceNote: AUTHORIZED STRUCTURAL EXCEPTION: correspondence records recurring difficulty and intention; it does not document a particular failed session. Letter159 follows the request and precedes the thanks.

arc.canonicalText: In another letter, he thanked the opera's writer for permission to keep the text. He repeated his promise to give a definite answer later that year. For now, he could keep it.
arc.sourceNote: AUTHORIZED STRUCTURAL EXCEPTION: letter160 proves permission and his written thanks, not its arrival time, location or an emotional transformation. No invented receipt scene.

arc.canonicalText: The following year, a concert deadline went unmet. He corrected a report that his new concerto was finished. He could not complete it in time and withdrew from the performance. Later, he sent two movements to a colleague to examine. The first movement was still unfinished. Months afterward, he played that movement and agreed with a friend's criticism. In his letter, he described despair near the performance. There was music, and doubt.
arc.sourceNote: Explicit compressed aftermath, letters175/178/186 in order. Continued work does not erase a missed deadline or criticism. No promised visit is converted into an actual meeting.

arc.canonicalText:
His name was Sergei Rachmaninoff.

He was a pianist and composer known for his Second Piano Concerto.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You are allowed to ask without certainty.
arc.sourceNote: Source-led correspondence vignette; the new stage and matching proposal require review and verified integration. No approval or publication is recorded.

dramatizationLimits: No invented piano-room scene, physical collapse, therapy dialogue, or private realization.
Same-day letters are separate documents; do not assume they were written in one uninterrupted sitting.
No clinical diagnosis or claim that a particular treatment guarantees restored creativity.
Do not replace the1873 birth date with an erroneous age in secondary concert notes.
Authorized source-led short form: seven schema roles do not certify four continuous moments or the full 700–950-word recipe.

Russian Senar transcriptions were read directly and paraphrased; manuscripts and a printed critical edition were not collated. This is a disclosed transmission limit, not fabricated independent translation approval.
The proposed 1900-1901-letters-and-unfinished-work stage and matching ages 27–28 follow the correspondence, replacing the old 1897–1901 / 23–28 humiliation-and-therapy framing.
avoidRules: Do not say he wrote literally nothing for three years; his June1900 letter explicitly excepts a song.
Do not assign a drunken state to the first-symphony conductor without direct evidence.
Do not claim the1900 libretto extension caused the later concerto.
Do not imply the opera and concerto are the same work.
Do not claim the Senar transcription is a facsimile or that unavailable manuscript originals were inspected.
